claims: Northern Lights are also known as aurora borealis.
Aurora borealis are caused by solar particles colliding with Earth’s magnetic field.
Peak Northern Lights activity is from 2024–2026.
Peak Northern Lights activity offers high visibility in Alaska, Canada, and Scandinavia.
Northern Lights are occasionally visible as far south as the U.S. Midwest during strong storms.
Northern Lights viewing season is August to May.
Northern Lights peak activity often occurs around the fall and spring equinoxes.
Northern Lights best viewing time is generally within an hour or two of midnight, between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m.
NOAA 30-Minute Aurora Forecast provides immediate visibility predictions.
Solar maximum is currently occurring.
Solar maximum is the peak of the sun's 11-year cycle.
Solar maximum produces more frequent and intense geomagnetic storms.
Solar maximum results in brighter, more colorful, and farther-south aurora displays.
Green is the most common color of aurora borealis, produced by oxygen.
Red and pink colors of aurora borealis can appear, produced by nitrogen.
Aurora borealis appear as arcs, streaks, or dancing, moving curtains of light.
Northern Lights hotspots in North America include Alaska, Canada, Washington, Montana, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Maine.
Northern Lights hotspots in Europe include Northern Norway, Sweden, Finland (e.g., Jukkasjärvi), and Iceland.
"G" classes are geomagnetic storms.
Higher "G" class numbers (e.g., G3-G5) mean better chances of aurora farther south
